analysis.one_liner: Sets a national goal of cutting U.S. carbon emissions 20% by 2000 through efficiency, renewables, and conservation programs.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 38 cosponsors, the bill never received a vote in any committee or on the House floor before the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would set a national goal of cutting U.S. carbon dioxide emissions at least 20% below 1988 levels by 2000 and negotiating a global atmosphere agreement by 1992. To get there, it funds energy-efficiency and renewable-energy research, requires home energy ratings and appliance efficiency standards, pushes utilities toward least-cost planning and paying customers to conserve, expands low-income weatherization, and ends the mandated logging program in Alaska's Tongass National Forest. It was referred to ten House committees, received unfavorable reviews from the Energy and Transportation Departments, and died without a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Households and renters would gain through lower energy bills from efficiency standards, appliance and lighting rules, window labels, home energy ratings at sale, and utility least-cost planning that treats conservation as a cheaper alternative to new power plants. Low-income homeowners would gain from an expanded weatherization program ($200 million authorized for fiscal 1991) with more flexible per-home spending. Emerging solar, wind, geothermal, fuel cell, and hydrogen industries would gain research funding, cost-reduction goals, and export financing. The public broadly would gain from reduced emissions, protection of the Tongass rainforest, tropical forest conditions on foreign aid, and international family planning funding.

how_it_helps.text: Writes into law a national goal of cutting U.S. carbon dioxide emissions at least 20% below 1988 levels by the year 2000, and of reaching a binding international agreement on the atmosphere by 1992.

Expands the low-income weatherization program, authorizing $200 million for fiscal 1991, letting the per-home spending cap rise with inflation, and letting states waive the 40-percent materials rule when audits show other measures save more energy.

Targets household energy bills directly: efficiency standards for incandescent and fluorescent lamps, labels for windows, an energy-efficiency rating assigned to every home at sale and shown to buyers and renters, and utility rates that must reward least-cost measures including conservation and demand reduction.

Requires electric utilities to buy verified conservation from third parties, much as they were already required to buy from small power producers, turning saved electricity into a resource that competes with building new generation.

Sets concrete cost goals for renewable energy — wind power at 3 to 5 cents per kilowatt-hour by 1995, photovoltaic modules at $800 per kilowatt — with multi-year funding for wind, solar, geothermal, biofuels, and ocean energy research, plus hydrogen and fuel cell programs.

Ends the automatic annual appropriations and long-term timber sale contracts for the Tongass National Forest and imposes a moratorium on timber sales until the forest plan is revised to protect old-growth, wildlife, and fisheries.

Ties foreign aid and U.S. votes at multilateral development banks to least-cost energy planning and tropical forest protection, authorizes debt relief conditioned on forest and energy conservation, and funds international family planning.

analysis.who_pays: Coal producers and coal-dependent utilities would bear the largest cost, since a 20% emissions cut and least-cost planning directly shrink coal demand, though the bill also funds clean coal and carbon-capture research. Oil companies would face programs explicitly aimed at cutting petroleum use and imports. The Alaska timber industry would lose the Tongass logging mandate, its long-term sale contracts, and sales during a moratorium. Electric and gas utilities would face least-cost hearings and mandatory conservation purchases that cut into sales. Taxpayers would fund the authorizations, which run to hundreds of millions of dollars a year across research, state programs, and demonstrations, and consumers in coal-reliant regions could see higher energy prices during the transition.
analysis.who_pays_short: Coal, oil, utilities, and timber companies

drawbacks.text: The bill relies heavily on plans, reports, studies, and advisory committees rather than enforceable mandates; the 20% emissions goal itself carries no penalty, so the bill's real-world effect would have depended on later legislation and agency follow-through.

The transition costs were real: the Tongass moratorium and contract terminations would have cost logging and mill jobs in southeast Alaska, and aggressive efficiency and fuel-switching would squeeze coal-mining regions and energy-intensive manufacturers.

It authorizes hundreds of millions of dollars in new federal spending each year across energy research, state conservation programs, and demonstration projects, and it would have layered new offices, boards, and subcommittees onto the Department of Energy.
The ban on importing wood from tropical countries that miss forest-plan goals could raise lumber and wood-product prices and would have been difficult to verify and enforce.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential gains for ordinary people were large — lower energy bills, a serious start on climate change, and an end to a subsidized old-growth logging program — while the main costs fell on fossil fuel producers, utilities, and the Alaska timber industry, with some genuine transition pain for coal towns and Alaska mill workers. The bill's biggest design weakness is that its centerpiece, the 20% emissions goal, is aspirational and enforced mostly through plans and reports; the enforceable parts (appliance standards, utility least-cost planning, weatherization, Tongass) are worthwhile but narrower. On balance a strong bill for energy consumers, though an honest supporter would admit the emissions target needed tools this bill did not provide.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat split among ten House committees and more than a dozen subcommittees, drew unfavorable written reviews from the Energy and Transportation Departments, and never got a committee or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Les AuCoin introduced the National Energy Policy Act of 1989 on August 4, 1989, with 38 cosponsors (37 Democrats and 1 Republican), and it was referred jointly to ten House committees at once.
Over the following weeks the bill was parceled out to more than a dozen subcommittees, and the Energy Department, Transportation Department, GSA, and OMB were asked for their views.
On October 5, 1989 the Department of Energy sent an unfavorable executive comment; on January 23, 1990 the Department of Transportation did the same.
No committee ever reported the bill and no vote was ever held in either chamber; it died when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal, oil, and electric utilities were better off because the bill died, since they avoided the 20% emissions goal, least-cost planning mandates, and required conservation purchases. The Alaska timber industry kept the Tongass logging appropriations and its long-term sale contracts.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coal, oil, utilities, and Alaska timber

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so the only measure of support is cosponsorship, which ran 37 Democrats to 1 Republican.

industries.note: A 20% cut in carbon emissions and least-cost planning that counts environmental costs would directly shrink coal demand, the industry's core market. The bill softens this with clean coal research funding and carbon capture and disposal programs, but the goal itself is the threat.

Utilities would face mandatory least-cost hearings, rates that must reward conservation, and required purchases of verified conservation from third parties, all of which cut into electricity sales. The bill also repeals the ban on utilities installing residential conservation measures, opening a new service line for them.

The bill repeals the ongoing appropriations for Tongass timber, terminates specified long-term sale contracts, and blocks timber sales until the forest plan is revised to protect old-growth, wildlife, and fisheries. Southeast Alaska mill towns bore the transition cost of ending a program the public subsidized.

The bill funds efficiency programs and fuel switching explicitly to cut petroleum consumption and oil imports, and requires evaluation of policies to cut energy use per unit of output each year through 2005.

industries.industry: Solar, wind, and renewable equipment makers
industries.note: Multi-year research funding, concrete cost targets (wind at 3-5 cents per kilowatt-hour, photovoltaics at $800 per kilowatt), federal procurement preferences, and set-asides in Export-Import Bank and small business lending would have built the industry's market.

The bill funds natural gas transit and fleet vehicle demonstrations, conversion training, Gas Research Institute research, and nonconventional gas recovery R&D, positioning gas as a lower-carbon fuel.
